Find which of the following matrices are invertible: (i) \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\)  (ii) \(B = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\)  (iii) \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\)
solution:
(i) As \(|A| = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = 0\), \(A\) is singular and hence \(A\) is not invertible.
(ii) As \(|B| = \begin{vmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{vmatrix} = \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1 \neq 0\), \(B\) is nonsingular, \(B\) is invertible.
(iii) \(|C| = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = -12 \neq 0\), \(C\) is nonsingular and hence \(C\) is invertible.

stem: Find the inverse of \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).
solution:
As \(|A| = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = -2\), \(|A| \neq 0\) so \(A^{-1}\) exists.
Let \(AA^{-1} = I\) (Here we can use only row transformation).
Using \(R_2 \to R_2 - 3R_1\), \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) becomes \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Using \(-\tfrac{1}{2}R_2\) we get \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \tfrac{3}{2} & -\tfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}\).
Using \(R_1 \to R_1 - 2R_2\), we get \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ \tfrac{3}{2} & -\tfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}\).
\(\therefore A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ \tfrac{3}{2} & -\tfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}\)

stem: Find the inverse of \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 6 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) by using elementary row transformations.
solution:
Consider \(|A| = 1 \neq 0\) so \(A^{-1}\) exists.
Consider \(AA^{-1} = I\), i.e. \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 6 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Use \(R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 6 \\ 2 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Use \(R_2 \to R_2 - 3R_1\) and \(R_3 \to R_3 - 2R_1\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Use \(R_2 \to -R_2\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Use \(R_1 \to R_1 - R_2\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Use \(R_1 \to R_1 - 2R_3\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(\therefore A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)

stem: Find the inverse of \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) by elementary column transformation.
solution:
As \(A^{-1}\) is required by column transformations we consider \(A^{-1}A = I\), i.e. \(A^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Using \(C_2 \to C_2 - 3C_1\) and \(C_3 \to C_3 - 3C_1\): \(A^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Use \(C_1 \to C_1 - C_2\): \(A^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -3 & -3 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Use \(C_1 \to C_1 - C_3\): \(A^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & -3 & -3 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(\therefore A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & -3 & -3 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)

If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), verify that \(A(\text{adj}\,A) = (\text{adj}\,A)A = |A|\,I\).
solution:
For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\):
\(A_{11} = (-1)^{1+1}(4) = 4\), \(A_{12} = (-1)^{1+2}(3) = -3\), \(A_{21} = (-1)^{2+1}(2) = -2\), \(A_{22} = (-1)^{2+2}(1) = 1\).
\(\text{adj}\,A = \begin{bmatrix} A_{11} & A_{21} \\ A_{12} & A_{22} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(\therefore A(\text{adj}\,A) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\)  ...(i)
\((\text{adj}\,A)A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\)  ...(ii)
And \(|A|\,I = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = (-2)\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\)  ...(iii)
From (i), (ii) and (iii) we get, \(A(\text{adj}\,A) = (\text{adj}\,A)A = |A|\,I\).

stem: Solve the equations \(2x + 5y = 1\) and \(3x + 2y = 7\) by the method of inversion.
solution: Using the given equations we get the corresponding matrix equation \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}\), i.e. \(AX = B\), where \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), \(X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}\). Premultiplying by \(A^{-1}\): \((A^{-1}A)X = A^{-1}B\), i.e. \(X = A^{-1}B\). Now \(|A| = -11\) and \(\text{adj } A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|}(\text{adj } A) = \dfrac{1}{-11}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\). Hence \(X = \dfrac{1}{-11}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{11}\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 5 \\ 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}\), i.e. \(\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{11}\begin{bmatrix} 33 \\ -11 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\). Hence by equality of matrices \(x = 3\) and \(y = -1\).

subtopic: Solution of Linear Equations using Matrices
stem: Solve the following equations by the method of inversion: \(x - y + z = 4,\ 2x + y - 3z = 0,\ x + y + z = 2\).
solution: The required matrix equation is \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\), i.e. \(AX = B\). Premultiplying by \(A^{-1}\) gives \(X = A^{-1}B\). Now \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), and by definition \(\text{adj } A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 & 2 \\ -5 & 0 & 5 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(|A| = 10\). So \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|}(\text{adj } A) = \dfrac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 & 2 \\ -5 & 0 & 5 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\). Hence \(X = \dfrac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 & 2 \\ -5 & 0 & 5 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix} 20 \\ -10 \\ 10 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Hence by equality of matrices \(x = 2,\ y = -1\) and \(z = 1\).

subtopic: Solution of Linear Equations using Matrices
stem: Solve the equations \(2x + 3y = 9\) and \(y - x = -2\) using the method of reduction.
solution: The given equations can be written as \(2x + 3y = 9\) and \(-x + y = -2\). Hence the matrix equation is \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}\) (i.e. \(AX = B\)). Now use \(R_2 \to 2R_2 + R_1\); we get \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}\). We rewrite the equations as \(2x + 3y = 9\) ... (i) and \(5y = 5\) ... (ii). From (ii) \(y = 1\) and using (i) we get \(x = 3\). Hence \(x = 3,\ y = 1\) is the required solution.

subtopic: Solution of Linear Equations using Matrices
stem: Solve the following equations by the method of reduction: \(x + 3y + 3z = 12,\ x + 4y + 4z = 15\) and \(x + 3y + 4z = 13\).
solution: The equations can be written in the form \(AX = B\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 4 \\ 1 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 12 \\ 15 \\ 13 \end{bmatrix}\). Using \(R_2 \to R_2 - R_1\) and \(R_3 \to R_3 - R_1\) we get \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 12 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Again using \(R_1 \to R_1 - 3R_2\) and \(R_2 \to R_2 - R_3\) we get \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Hence the required solution is \(x = 3,\ y = 2,\ z = 1\).

subtopic: Solution of Linear Equations using Matrices
stem: Solve the following equations by the method of reduction: \(x + y + z = 1,\ 2x + 3y + 2z = 2\) and \(x + y + 2z = 4\).
solution: The equations can be written in the form \(AX = B\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}\). Using \(R_2 \to R_2 - R_3\) and \(R_1 \to R_1 - \dfrac{1}{2}R_3\) we get \(\begin{bmatrix} \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ -2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}\). Now using \(R_1 \to R_1 - \dfrac{1}{4}R_2\) we get \(\begin{bmatrix} \tfrac{1}{4} & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\tfrac{1}{2} \\ -2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}\). Here A is reduced to a lower triangular matrix. Rewriting the equations: \(\dfrac{x}{4} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) ... (i), i.e. \(x = -2\); \(x + 2y = -2\) ... (ii), so \(2y = -2 + 2 = 0\), \(y = 0\); and \(x + y + 2z = 4\), so \(2z = 4 + 2 + 0 = 6\), \(z = 3\). Hence \(x = -2,\ y = 0,\ z = 3\) is the required solution.

subtopic: Solution of Linear Equations using Matrices
stem: The cost of 2 books and 6 note books is Rs. 34 and the cost of 3 books and 4 notebooks is Rs. 31. Using matrices, find the cost of one book and one note-book.
solution: Let Rs. \(x\) and Rs. \(y\) be the costs of one book and one notebook respectively. Then \(2x + 6y = 34\) and \(3x + 4y = 31\). These can be expressed as \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 6 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 34 \\ 31 \end{bmatrix}\) (i.e. \(AX = B\)). Using \(R_2 \to R_2 - \dfrac{3}{2}R_1\) we get \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 6 \\ 0 & -5 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 34 \\ -20 \end{bmatrix}\). As A is reduced to an upper triangular matrix, the equations are \(2x + 6y = 34\) and \(-5y = -20\), so \(y = 4\); and \(2x = 34 - 6y = 34 - 24 = 10\), so \(x = 5\). Hence the cost of a book is Rs. 5 and that of a note book is Rs. 4.
